protocol.instrument_name: Protocol for Management of Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
protocol.legal_basis: Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981 and Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulations 2017 (Victoria); Secretary Approval: Community Pharmacist Statewide Pilot. Supply of the Schedule 4 poisons documented in this Protocol for the purpose of managing herpes zoster (HZ) under a structured prescribing arrangement. Requirement of the Secretary Approval: Community Pharmacist Statewide Pilot that pharmacists comply with this Protocol and have completed the designated pharmacist training requirements specified in the departmental guidance before supplying the Schedule 4 poisons. Pharmacists must operate at all times in accordance with the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981, the Regulations and all other applicable Victorian, Commonwealth and national laws, and act consistently with the Pharmacy Board of Australia's Code of Conduct. HZ is a nationally notifiable disease requiring notification to the Victorian Department of Health within 5 days.
protocol.supervision_model: structured prescribing arrangement (pharmacists authorised under the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulations 2017 to supply Schedule 4 poisons documented in the Protocol; must comply with the Protocol and have completed the designated pharmacist training requirements specified in the departmental guidance before supplying the Schedule 4 poisons)
protocol.scope_summary: Victorian Community Pharmacist Statewide Pilot protocol (February 2024) for management of herpes zoster (shingles). Covers eligibility (aged 18 years or over, consent with patient physically present in the pharmacy, HZ signs confirmed), an eligibility/referral flowchart (ear, eye and nose involvement; unclear diagnosis; >2 dermatomes/midline; genital rash; superinfection; complications; antiviral allergy; pregnancy/VZV status; breastfeeding; immunocompromise; rash duration), conservative analgesia, empirical antiviral therapy (valaciclovir, famciclovir, aciclovir) with a 72-hour rule for immunocompetent patients, communication/documentation requirements, mandatory notification of HZ cases to the Victorian Department of Health within 5 days, supplementary assessment guidance (presenting signs, complications, patient history, examination), referral points summary, vaccination and transmission advice, and clinical review at 48-72 hours.

steps.description: CONDUCT CLINICAL REVIEW - Examination: 'Confirm presenting signs and symptoms indicative of HZ including a rash characterised by pain and blistering which usually appears on one side of the face/body and does not cross the body's midline.' 'When examining patients, standard and contact precautions apply for cases of localised HZ'; 'PPE including gloves, gowns and/or masks should be used, and surfaces should be cleaned with neutral detergent and disinfectant after examination'; 'Ensure hand hygiene is being performed'.

Yes: 'Immediate referral to General Practitioner for urgent review or local Emergency Department to confirm presence of HZ'. No: continue to the next question.

gates.criterion: No hearing loss, hyperacusis, tinnitus or otalgia without identifiable rash, and no other symptoms suggesting Herpes Zoster Oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)

steps.description: Question: 'Does the patient have vesicular rash in or around the ear that can be confirmed as HZ?'. 'No: continue to page 5' (printed protocol page number; PDF page 7).

gates.criterion: No vesicular rash in or around the ear that can be confirmed as HZ

steps.description: Question: 'Does the patient report a rash affecting the eye or other symptoms suggesting Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus?' with 'Skin symptoms can include acute vesicular rash that is unilateral' and 'Ocular symptoms can include pain, redness, watering, photophobia, blurred/decreased vision'. Yes: 'Refer to the Emergency Department'. Note: 'If rash affecting the eye has been present >72 hours, critical to have urgent ophthalmologist review if feasible. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist through General Practitioner or immediate referral to Emergency Department. If availability or location is an issue, a review by an optometrist may be appropriate.' No: continue.

gates.criterion: No rash affecting the eye and no other symptoms suggesting Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus

steps.description: Question: 'Does the patient report / present with any of the following? l Patient is immunocompromised or taking immunosuppressant medicines (regardless of the time lapsed since rash onset) l Rash indicative of HZ affecting areas other than torso but excluding eye and ear (see above) l Patient presents with complications of HZ including: – PHN – Disseminated zoster (VZV dissemination): Whilst most individuals have some lesions external to the primary dermatome, disseminated zoster is defined as 20 lesions outside of the dermatome and may be clinically indistinguishable from varicella infection. l Patient is requiring pain management for neuropathic pain or moderate to severe nociceptive pain associated with HZ or PHN l Patient is pregnant and has a definite history of previous VZV – Refer to treating obstetrician or shared care GP (also refer to perform urgent serology if uncertain of history of previous VZV) l Patient has been previously vaccinated against HZ l Patient is breastfeeding a baby aged over one month – Rash needs to be covered to reduce exposure to the baby, however noting this may cause difficulty in breastfeeding if HZ is affecting the breast'. Yes: 'Refer to General Practitioner' with care-column note 'Antiviral treatment by pharmacist may still be considered if clinically appropriate. go to: ANTIVIRAL THERAPY section on page 8 below.'. 'No: continue to page 8' (printed protocol page number; PDF page 10).

steps.description: PHARMACIST CARE / PHARMACOTHERAPY. Question: 'Does the patient have allergies, drug-drug interactions or any other contraindications to management options?'. Yes: 'Where antiviral therapy is considered the appropriate treatment option but all recommended antivirals under this protocol are contraindicated, refer patient to General Practitioner' (the document does not state the action when only some options are contraindicated). No: continue to the rash-duration gate.

gates.criterion: No allergies, drug-drug interactions or other contraindications to management options

steps.description: Question: 'Has rash been present for longer than 72 hours? (For immunocompetent patients only)'. Yes: 'Conservative management including symptomatic treatment with non-prescription medicines (if appropriate) can be recommended. Refer to General Practitioner following provisional treatment by pharmacist'. No: 'CONSIDER ANTIVIRAL THERAPY - Provide antiviral therapy, where indicated: l Valaciclovir (1st line) 1g orally, every 8 hours for 7 days (42 x 500mg tablets) OR l Famciclovir (1st line) 500mg orally, every 8 hours for 7 days (21 x 500mg tablets); 10 days for immunocompromised (30 x 500mg tablets) OR l Aciclovir (2nd line) 800mg orally, 5 times a day for 7 days (35 x 800mg tablets)'. 'Dispense medications via pharmacy dispensing software and label according to the legislative requirements outlined in the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled substances Regulation 2017'. 'Continue to page 9' (printed protocol page number; PDF page 11).

gates.criterion: Rash has not been present for longer than 72 hours (immunocompetent patients only)
Antiviral therapy where indicated: immunocompetent adults present within 72 hours of the onset of the rash, or patient is immunocompromised regardless of the time lapsed since rash onset

steps.description: 'Provide conservative management with non-prescription analgesia for mild acute nociceptive HZ pain: l Paracetamol 1g orally, every 4-6 hours as required. Maximum dose of 4g in 24 hours AND/OR l Ibuprofen 200-400mg orally, every 6-8 hours as required. Maximum dose of 2.4g in 24 hours AND/OR l Lidocaine 5% patch, up to 3 patches applied at the same time to the painful area (after shingles has healed). Wear for up to 12 hours, followed by a patch-free interval; l Advise patient regarding follow-up for HZ vaccination at a later date; l Provide non-pharmacological and supportive management advice – Care of lesions i.e., applying hydrogels such as Solugel™ or Solosite™ for lesions – Transmission and infectious precautions required until skin lesions have healed'.

steps.description: 'Communicate agreed treatment plan: l Treatment and management recommendations l Counselling for antivirals and analgesics, including adverse effects l Duration of treatment and expectations around duration of symptoms l General health advice l Infection control advice/outbreak measures l Recommendations for vaccination l Communicate with other health practitioners (especially high-risk patients such as immunocompromised patients, pregnant patients)'. 'Document the consultation and share a record of the service with the patient, patient's usual treating GP or medical practice where the patient has one'. 'Continue to page 10' (printed protocol page number; PDF page 12).

'Notify the Victorian Department of Health of HZ case within 5 days of initial consultation (see Section 3 for more information)'.

gates.criterion: Follow-up/clinical review provided (progression of rash, worsening signs/symptoms, complications including PHN, adverse effects, communication with other health practitioners, HZ vaccination follow-up plan)

diagnosis_pathways.name: Supplementary information: assess patient needs, manage, communicate and review (pg. 15-22)

steps.description: 4.1. PRESENTING SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS - Prodromal symptoms 'may be observed between 48-72 hours before the localised, characteristic vesicular rash becomes evident' (localised nerve pain - stabbing, prickling or burning; lethargy, fever, headache; abnormal skin sensations; photophobia (approximately 80% of cases)). 'The HZ rash is typically unilateral with a dermatomal distribution and distinct anterior and posterior midline cut-offs'; 'New lesions will continue to erupt for 3 to 5 days ... becoming pustular, before scabbing and crusting over between 7 to 10 days.' Ophthalmicus: 'Assessment within 24-48 hours by an ophthalmologist in the community or the Emergency Department at The Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital is recommended. If availability or location is an issue, a review by an optometrist may be appropriate within the same timeframe.' Oticus/Ramsay Hunt: 'symptoms include facial paralysis, ear pain, tinnitus' plus hearing loss, blistering in and around the ear canal, vertigo, change in taste sensation, dry eye, tearing, hyperacusis, nasal obstruction, hoarseness or aspiration and dysarthria.

4.2. COMPLICATIONS OF HZ - 'Complications occur in approximately 13-26% of patients with HZ (most prevalent in older people and those who are immunocompromised) and will require referral to a medical practitioner at presentation.' Complications: Postherpetic neuralgia ('Neuropathic pain that persists for at least 3 months beyond the duration of the rash', occurs in 10-50% of patients); Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (10-25% of cases; keratitis, conjunctivitis, uveitis, retinitis, glaucoma; 'Vesicles on the nose have been found to be predictive of eye involvement'); Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome); Disseminated zoster ('defined as 20 lesions outside of the dermatome'; 'Viral dissemination to the central nervous system and viscera (lungs, gut, liver, and brain) may occur'; 'Airborne infection controls are required, and individuals should call ahead before attending a healthcare facility'); Other complications - 'Neurological complications such as meningoencephalitis and myelitis (particularly in the elderly)', 'Secondary bacterial skin infections (referral to a medical practitioner for swab and skin culture is required)', 'Scarring', 'Pneumonia'. HZ in pregnancy: 'Pregnant women who are exposed to VZV (chicken pox or HZ) for the first time (no or uncertain history of previous chicken pox infection) ... They must urgently be referred to a shared care medical practitioner (including an emergency service), treating obstetrician or pregnancy service immediately, as zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) should be given to all seronegative women within 96 hours.'

gates.criterion: No complications of HZ at presentation (including PHN, HZ ophthalmicus, HZ oticus, disseminated zoster, neurological complications, secondary bacterial skin infections, scarring, pneumonia) and no first-time VZV exposure in pregnancy

steps.description: 4.3. PATIENT HISTORY - 'Sufficient information must be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines for the patient. Consider:' age; 'pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable)'; nature, severity and frequency of symptoms; nature of rash (distribution, appearance, number of lesions); onset and duration of symptoms; precipitating and relieving factors; history of VZV infection; co-existing and underlying medical conditions 'e.g., immunocompromise or auto-immune diseases including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV, cancer, conditions treated with immune suppressants, or renal impairment'; current medications (prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse drug effects; medication and other strategies tried to treat current symptoms; 'immunisation status as per the Australian Immunisation Handbook (zoster and varicella vaccinations)'.

4.4. EXAMINATION - 'Examination of the rash and documentation of its characteristics and location, as well as any signs of complications is important for the diagnosis of HZ and the exclusion of other conditions with similar presentations.' 'Apply standard and contact infection precautions when examining patients.' 'Laboratory confirmation is generally not required for typical presentations and uncomplicated cases of HZ. Confirmatory pathology testing (initiated by a medical practitioner) is required for cases where diagnosis is uncertain, or in cases of HZ in people who have been previously vaccinated against HZ.'

gates.criterion: Typical presentation and uncomplicated case of HZ (laboratory confirmation generally not required)

steps.description: 5. Management and treatment plan - 'Antiviral treatment can reduce acute pain, duration of the rash, viral shedding, and ocular complications, if commenced within 72 hours of the first appearance of the rash but is not indicated in all patients.' Supportive management: education and advice regarding care for lesions (dressings, hydrogel, cleaning, appropriate clothing) and transmission precautions per the Victorian Department of Health's webpage – Chickenpox and shingles (varicella/herpes zoster). Pharmacotherapy: 'Antiviral therapy in accordance with Shingles [published 2019 April; amended 2022 May]. In: Therapeutic Guidelines. Antiviral therapy is indicated for: Immunocompetent adults who present within 72 hours of the onset of the rash; All immunocompromised patients (including those with a HIV infection) regardless of the time lapsed since rash onset'. 'Analgesia for mild nociceptive HZ pain in accordance with Acute pain associated with shingles (herpes zoster) and Mild, acute nociceptive pain [2020 December]. In: Therapeutic Guidelines (i.e., oral paracetamol, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or Lidocaine patch.' 'Patients reporting neuropathic pain or moderate to severe nociceptive pain must be referred to a medical practitioner.'

gates.criterion: For antiviral therapy: immunocompetent adult presents within 72 hours of the onset of the rash, OR patient is immunocompromised (including those with a HIV infection) regardless of the time lapsed since rash onset
Pain is mild nociceptive HZ pain (not neuropathic pain or moderate to severe nociceptive pain)

steps.description: 5.1. CONFIRM MANAGEMENT IS APPROPRIATE - 'Pharmacists must consult Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references to confirm the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: l Contraindications and precautions l Drug interactions l Pregnancy and lactation'.

gates.criterion: Treatment recommendation confirmed appropriate for contraindications and precautions, drug interactions, and pregnancy and lactation

steps.description: 5.2. COMMUNICATE AGREED MANAGEMENT PLAN - 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references should be provided to the patient regarding: l Medicine use e.g. dosing l How to manage adverse effects l Infection control advice/outbreak measures l Recommendations for vaccination against HZ l When to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising superinfection and HZ complications l When to return to the pharmacist for clinical review'. 5.2.1 General advice: patient resources (Better Health Channel Shingles; HealthDirect shingles page); 'All patients should be advised to contact a medical practitioner if: – They are not responding to treatment; and/or – Their condition worsens; and/or – They are experiencing complications (as soon as the complications become evident) such as: Secondary bacterial infections; Pain not relieved by non-prescription analgesia; Rash begins to affect areas other than torso including eye(s), ear(s) or forehead'; 'The incubation period of VZV ranges between 10 and 21 days (14 to 16 days on average).'; 'Skin lesions usually heal within 2-4 weeks'; recovery complete in 2 to 4 weeks in most cases.

Preventing transmission - 'The patient should be advised to inform any high-risk contacts (pregnant patients, patients who are breastfeeding a neonate, neonates in first month of life and immunocompromised individuals) who have had significant exposure to a person with active VZV (household contacts or where there has been direct face-to-face contact for 5 minutes or being within the same room for at least an hour) to seek medical care as soon as possible.' 'People with HZ are infectious from 1-2 days prior to the onset of the rash, until vesicles have dried and scabbed (usually 5 days after the onset of the rash).' 'Rashes should be covered with appropriate dressings until the person is no longer infectious and contact with pregnant women and immunocompromised people must be avoided.'

5.2.2 Zoster vaccination - 'Vaccination against HZ is the best way to prevent HZ and reduce the risk of complications but is not indicated during an acute HZ episode or to treat PHN.' 'generally immunocompetent patients should wait 12 months after an episode of HZ before they receive an HZ vaccine, while immunocompromised patients can receive Shingrix from 3 months after experiencing an HZ episode.' 'From 1 November 2023, Shringrix replaced Zostavax on the NIP schedule for the prevention of shingles and PHN.' (printed as 'Shringrix'). Zoster vaccines recommended for (unless contraindicated): 'Immunocompetent people ≥ 50 years'; 'Immunocompromised people ≥ 18 years'; 'People aged ≥ 50 years who are household contacts of an immunocompromised person'; 'Before administering a zoster vaccine, the pharmacist must consult the Australian Immunisation Handbook – Zoster and the NCIRS Zoster vaccines for Australian adults factsheet.'

6. Follow-up/clinical review - 'Clinical review with the pharmacist should occur in line with recommendations in Therapeutic Guidelines and other relevant guidelines. Clinical review is recommended 48-72 hours after the initial presentation to assess for: l Progression of the rash (particularly if the patient presented with prodromal symptoms prior to rash onset) l Worsening of clinical signs and symptoms including neuropathic pain l Screening for complications of HZ l Adverse effects'. 'During any follow up consultation with the patient, the pharmacist should provide advice regarding vaccination against further HZ infections. Noting for immunocompetent patients, this should occur at least 12 months after the infection and from 3 months for immunocompromised patients.' 'Where subsequent HZ vaccination has been administered, pharmacist immunisers should also provide follow up advice to patients. Refer to 'After vaccination' guidance in the Australian Immunisation Handbook.'

gates.criterion: Clinical review occurs 48-72 hours after the initial presentation to assess progression of rash, worsening of clinical signs and symptoms including neuropathic pain, complications of HZ and adverse effects

treatments.quantity_to_supply: 42 x 500mg tablets (pack size printed in flowchart, p10)
treatments.notes: 1st line. Table dose printed as '1 g orally, 8-hourly for 7 days'; flowchart (p10) prints 'Valaciclovir (1st line) 1g orally, every 8 hours for 7 days (42 x 500mg tablets)'. Contraindications: 'Previous serious adverse reaction to valaciclovir or its active metabolite aciclovir'. 'Empirical antiviral therapy where indicated' - 'If the rash has been present for less than 72 hours, antiviral treatment reduces acute pain, duration of the rash, viral shedding, and ocular complications.' Pregnancy (p24, verbatim): 'Valaciclovir: Metabolised rapidly to aciclovir. Limited information available.' ('Aciclovir: Preferred as there is more clinical experience and greater number of published studies available.'). Breastfeeding (p24, verbatim): 'Valaciclovir: Metabolised rapidly to aciclovir. Small amounts are excreted into breast milk, but these amounts are unlikely to pose harm to the breastfed infant. Considered safe to use during breastfeeding.' Pregnancy/breastfeeding source: The Royal Women's Hospital Pregnancy and Breastfeeding Medicines Guide, 2023.

treatments.duration: 7 days. For immunocompromised patients, duration is 10 days
treatments.quantity_to_supply: 21 x 500mg tablets for 7 days; 30 x 500mg tablets for 10 days for immunocompromised (pack sizes printed in flowchart, p10)

For immunocompromised patients, duration is 10 days'; flowchart (p10) prints 'Famciclovir (1st line) 500mg orally, every 8 hours for 7 days (21 x 500mg tablets); 10 days for immunocompromised (30 x 500mg tablets)'. Contraindications: 'Previous serious adverse reaction to famciclovir or its active metabolite penciclovir'. Pregnancy (p24, printed as 'Famiciclovir'): 'Famiciclovir: Limited information.' ('Aciclovir: Preferred as there is more clinical experience and greater number of published studies available.'). Breastfeeding (p24, verbatim): 'Famiciclovir: No published reports describing the use of famiciclovir during breastfeeding and effects of famciclovir in breastfed infants is unknown.
